findings.title: `_latest_bar_dt` removal changes the trailing-weekend tolerance predicate without an equivalent guard for the *pre-market* tail
findings.description: The old code accepted a PARTIAL as SUCCESS when the latest bar's date was within 4 days of `chunk_end.date()`. The replacement judges by session bounds fetched from `trading_sessions` for `[chunk_start, chunk_end]`. For a chunk that spans a session whose `session_open_utc` is inside the chunk but whose `session_close_utc` is after `chunk_end`, `sessions_without_bars` skips it (`session_close > chunk_end`) — correct. But for a chunk that ends *before* a session's open (e.g. a gap row ending at midnight for a session that opens at 13:30 the same day), `fetch_session_bounds` filters on `session_open_utc >= from_ts AND session_open_utc <= to_ts`, so the session is included with `close > chunk_end` and skipped as "cut through" — also fine. The residual gap is the *pre-market* side: a chunk whose only bars fall before the session open (EODHD's 08:00–13:30 UTC extended-hours bars) now yields an empty `judged` list only when no session closes within the chunk; in that case `judge_chunk_by_sessions` keeps the classifier's verdict (`SUCCESS` from `classify_outcome`'s date comparison), so a pre-market-only response can still delete the gap row. The new module's docstring claims the predicate "subsumes the former trailing-weekend tolerance", but it does not cover the pre-market-only case, which the old 4-day date tolerance also did not. Worth a stated argument (or a test) that pre-market-only bars never satisfy a session and never reach `SUCCESS` — currently `judge_chunk_by_sessions` returns the classifier verdict unchanged when `judged` is empty.

findings.title: `cagg_freshness_for_session` reads `max(created_at)` from the raw hypertable with no `symbol` predicate and no statement timeout
findings.description: The freshness probe scans `minute_ohlcv` across the whole session window (potentially ~50k–2M rows for a full session) with `WHERE time >= %s AND time <= %s` and no `symbol` filter — the filter is not needed (it wants the newest write anywhere in the session) but the query has no `SET LOCAL statement_timeout`, unlike the sibling `fetch_session_mass` (which sets `HEALTH_MINUTE_SESSION_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT`) and unlike `build_truncated_day_index` (which sets `TRUNCATION_SCAN_TIMEOUT`). The `minute_ohlcv` hypertable has 7-day chunks; a session window sits inside one chunk, so this is bounded, but the read is on the "§166/§167 latency cliff" table the surrounding code is careful to avoid, and `--verify` runs it on every poll. Add an explicit timeout consistent with the neighbouring reads.

findings.title: The freshness probe's `stale` verdict compares a refresh *finish* against a bar *write* time, so an hourly refresh that ran after the write but before the cagg materialized the bucket is judged fresh
findings.description: `CaggFreshness.stale` is `last_refresh < newest_bar_written`. `last_successful_finish` is when the policy *finished*, which is after the bucket containing the bar was materialized only if that bucket was inside the policy's window and fully closed. Two cases make this false-negative: (a) the bar was written *during* the refresh run (so `created_at` < finish but the row was not in the refresh's invalidation set), and (b) the session's bucket was still the *open* 4-hour bucket at refresh time and is therefore never re-materialized while open — the exact structural limitation documented at length in `constants.py` (`COVERAGE_BUCKET_LAG_BUDGET`, `COVERAGE_CONTENT_STALENESS`). In case (b) the cagg can be an hour or more behind while the probe says "fresh", and `--verify` then judges a truncated mass. The probe's own docstring says "Neither application role owns the cagg, so the probe cannot refresh it", which is true, but the verdict is then optimistic on the most common shape of lag. A safer predicate would compare against the cagg's own edge (e.g. `max(time_bucket)` of the H4 view for the session window) rather than only the policy's finish timestamp — the repo already has `assert_cagg_fresh` for exactly this class of question and it is not consulted here.

findings.title: `judge_chunk_by_sessions` promotes a PARTIAL to SUCCESS, which deletes the gap row even when only one bar of a 390-minute session was fetched
findings.description: The satisfaction predicate is "any bar in `(open, close]`". A chunk that returns a single bar (say the 09:31 minute of a 13:30–20:00 session) satisfies the session, so `judge_chunk_by_sessions` returns `SUCCESS`, and `_advance_minute_gap` **deletes** the gap row — the exact failure mode this slice exists to remove (a truncated session reading as collected). The repair's own truncated-day predicate is stricter (`max(time) <= session_open_utc` = not collected), so the two are not in agreement for anything between "one bar at the open" and "one bar at the close", contradicting the module docstring's claim that "the daemon and the repair agree on what a truncated session is". A minimum bar count per session (or comparing the bar count to the session's minute count) would keep the row for a partially-collected session.

findings.title: `fetch_session_bounds` is issued once per chunk with a fresh pool connection, doubling the DB round trips of the chunk loop
findings.description: Each chunk now opens a separate `pool.connection()` to read the symbol's session bounds for `[chunk_start, chunk_end]`. At ~13k symbols per trailing pass (and far more in backfill) this is one extra query plus one extra pool checkout per chunk, on a path whose whole purpose was to cut provider calls. `fetch_session_bounds` takes `(conn, symbol, from_ts, to_ts)` and could be satisfied from a per-symbol calendar cached for the pass (the session calendar is a small, slowly-changing table), or the bounds could be fetched once per symbol and reused across that symbol's chunks. As written the backfill phase pays the extra query on every chunk of every symbol.

findings.title: The new sudoers file grants the operator NOPASSWD `cat /etc/manta-trading.env` and `mt-run *`
findings.description: `MT_READ = /usr/bin/cat /etc/manta-trading.env` with `NOPASSWD` hands the `manta` account the production credentials (EODHD API key, database URLs) in cleartext, without a password. The file's own header claims "Exactly the commands those scripts issue, nothing wider", but reading the env file is not a command any of the cutover scripts issue through `sudo` — `cutover_common.migrate` reads it with `out(["cat", str(ENV_FILE)], sudo=True)` (that is the one), but `cat` of a root-owned 0640 secrets file is a broad grant (the value of every secret in it) and the `manta` user is the operator account. `MT_RUN = /usr/local/bin/mt-run *` is equally broad: `mt-run` is a wrapper that runs the production `mt` CLI with the credentials (`run_production_mt`), so `sudo mt-run <anything>` is effectively unrestricted production access — including `mt data migrate apply`, which the slice's own runbook treats as a gated action. Consider narrowing to the specific subcommands the cutover issues, and dropping or gating the env-file read.

findings.title: The cutover's `fire_unit_until` stops the systemd unit, which cancels the in-flight pass mid-chunk
findings.description: `fire_unit_until` stops `mt-minute-pass.service` as soon as the "trailing phase complete" journal line appears, precisely to bound an otherwise-unbounded backfill. The unit's `TimeoutStopSec=300` and the runner's SIGTERM handling mean the trailing phase's own last symbol may be interrupted (the runner exits between symbols), so a trailing phase that completes its *walk* but not its final symbol's fetch can be cut short. The next timer firing covers it, which is what the comment says, but the acceptance run then measures a session that was deliberately not collected — worth confirming the cutover's `--verify` accounting distinguishes "not collected yet" (WAIT) from "truncated" (FAIL) in that window. As written `run_verify` treats a fresh-enough cagg with a low mass as FAIL.

findings.title: `install()` now resolves the installer path from `__file__`, but `preflight()` still checks the relative `deploy/install-production.sh`
findings.description: `preflight` refuses unless `Path("deploy/install-production.sh").exists()` — a relative path, so the script must be run from the checkout root — while `install` now uses an absolute path derived from `Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]`. Both are correct in the intended workflow, but the two spellings of the same file differ; if the script is ever run from another directory the preflight message ("run from the dev checkout root") and the installer path disagree about which file is meant. Minor, but it is the same class of drift the `install` change was meant to remove.

findings.title: `say()` opens and appends the log file on every call
findings.description: Each `say` reopens the file for append. For a cutover that narrates a handful of lines this is irrelevant, but the narration is the point of the change, and a `with` block per line is needless churn. Holding the handle open (or buffering) would be simpler; the current form is nevertheless correct and safe if the process dies.

findings.title: The session-judgement predicate is correctly unit-tested against the real EODHD spillover shape
findings.description: `test_minute_sessions.py` covers the epoch/`datetime` bar shapes, the "bar at the open does not satisfy" boundary, the "previous session's bars do not satisfy the next" case, the chunk-cuts-through case, and the outcomes that must pass through unchanged. This matches the project's parsing rule (the fixture uses the real payload shape, including the ISO `datetime` string alongside the epoch `timestamp`) and pins the exact regression that motivated the change.

findings.title: The truncated-day seeding path is fail-safe and logged at ERROR when the scan times out
findings.description: `_build_truncated_index` catches `RepairScanTimeout` specifically, logs with `_logger.exception`, and returns `None` so the cycle seeds without the index — the same "coverage unavailable" semantics the coverage index uses, and never a silent full-window re-seed. The test asserts the `logger.exception` call and the `None` return.

findings.title: The `[WAIT]` verdict is never treated as acceptance
findings.description: `_verify_when_fresh` re-polls while the repair prints `[WAIT]` and the acceptance checks in both the loop and the final report exclude `"[WAIT]"`, so a stale cagg cannot be read as a pass. The test `test_a_wait_verdict_never_counts_as_acceptance` pins it end-to-end.

findings.title: The firing-time constant, the timer file, and the health check stay in agreement
findings.description: `MINUTE_PASS_FIRING_TIMES_UTC = (time(4, 5), time(13, 5))` matches the timer's two `OnCalendar` lines, and `test/unit/deploy/test_units.py` parses the timer and asserts the match — the drift guard the slice design called for is in place, and the 01:05 → 04:05 change was applied to all three copies (constant, timer, health-check docstrings and tests) rather than to one.
